analysis.one_liner: Bans drug middlemen from pocketing the gap between what insurers pay and pharmacies get.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill to ban pharmacy middlemen's hidden markups and pharmacy pay clawbacks cleared the Senate Commerce Committee with 14 cosponsors from both parties, then sat on the Senate calendar for more than a year and never got a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) are companies that run prescription drug benefits for insurers and employers. This bill would make it illegal for a PBM to charge a health plan more for a drug than it pays the pharmacy and keep the difference, to 'claw back' money it already paid a pharmacy, or to cut pharmacy pay to offset federal reimbursement changes. A PBM could avoid the ban only by passing 100% of every rebate and discount to the health plan and fully disclosing its costs, fees, and markups. The bill also requires PBMs to report their spread pricing and fees to the Federal Trade Commission each year, directs government studies of PBM practices, protects whistleblowers, and lets the FTC and state attorneys general enforce the rules with penalties up to $1 million per violation.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients with prescription drug coverage, who could see lower out-of-pocket drug costs if PBM fees and spread pricing end; employers, unions, and government programs that buy drug coverage, who would learn what they are actually paying; and independent and community pharmacies, many of which lose money on prescriptions filled at PBM-set reimbursement rates. The bill's exception channel also leaves PBMs in place as the permanent middlemen of the drug supply chain if they comply.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it unlawful for a PBM to charge a health plan a different amount for a drug's cost or dispensing fee than it reimburses the pharmacy, where the PBM keeps the difference.

The bill bars PBMs from arbitrarily, unfairly, or deceptively clawing back payments already made to pharmacies, unless the original claim was fraudulent, contradicted the contract, or the service was not actually rendered.
The bill bars PBMs from raising fees or cutting pharmacy reimbursement to offset reimbursement changes the federal government orders in federally funded health plans.

A PBM escapes the ban only if it passes along 100% of every price concession, rebate, or discount to the health plan and fully discloses its costs, fees, markups, and the payments it receives from drug manufacturers.

PBMs must report annually to the FTC and HHS the gap between what they charge plans and pay pharmacies, the fees and clawbacks charged to pharmacies, why they move drugs to higher-cost formulary tiers, and any difference in how they treat pharmacies they own versus other pharmacies.

The FTC can enforce the bill with civil penalties of up to $1 million per violation, with each day of a continuing violation counted separately, and state attorneys general can sue on behalf of their residents.

The bill protects whistleblowers at PBMs, insurers, drugmakers, and pharmacies from being fired or retaliated against for reporting violations, and blocks predispute arbitration agreements from waiving that protection.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers — including the large ones owned by CVS, Cigna, and UnitedHealth — would lose revenue from spread pricing, clawbacks, and opaque fees if the bill became law. Some of that cost could be passed to health plans in the form of changed PBM fees, though the bill's pass-through requirement is designed to push those savings back to plans and patients.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and their corporate owners

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves the PBM middleman structure in place: a PBM that passes 100% of rebates through and discloses its fees can keep operating as before, so the rebate system that pushes drug list prices up remains rather than being dismantled.
The maximum civil penalty is $1 million per violation, which is small against the multi-billion-dollar revenues of the largest PBMs, so the fines may not change behavior by themselves.
The bill does not directly cap drug prices or patients' out-of-pocket costs; it relies on transparency and enforcement to change prices indirectly.

PBMs would have an affirmative defense in enforcement actions if they show the conduct was reasonably necessary to comply with law, protect patient safety, or protect patient access, which gives companies room to contest penalties.

Good-faith objection from the industry side: full public disclosure of negotiated prices and rebates could expose commercially sensitive terms and, PBMs argue, might not lower drug costs if manufacturers simply raise list prices to keep rebate levels intact.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main gain — ending spread pricing and clawbacks that squeeze both patients and pharmacies — is real and directly aimed at practices documented in the bill's own findings and enforcement targets. The main limitation is that the bill regulates PBMs rather than restructuring the rebate system, and its penalty ceiling is modest relative to the size of the industry. On balance, for ordinary people the bill offered more benefit than cost; the larger cost fell on PBM companies.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce Committee approved the bill and it was placed on the Senate's business calendar in December 2023, but the Senate never brought it up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Maria Cantwell introduced the bill on January 26, 2023, with a bipartisan group of original cosponsors including Senator Chuck Grassley.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
On March 22, 2023, the committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute.

On December 13, 2023, Senator Cantwell reported the bill to the full Senate with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 283.
The bill never received a floor vote in the Senate, and no further action occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers and their parent companies — including CVS, Cigna, and UnitedHealth — kept the spread pricing, clawbacks, and opaque fees the bill would have banned, because the Senate never voted on it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support was bipartisan from the start: a Democratic sponsor with 14 cosponsors split 10 Republicans and 4 Democrats, and the bill cleared a Senate committee in both a March markup and a December report.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers (including the PBM units of CVS, Cigna, and UnitedHealth)
industries.note: The bill would ban spread pricing, clawbacks, and opaque fees that are a core revenue source for PBMs, and would subject them to FTC enforcement and annual disclosure. Its transparency-and-pass-through exception would leave PBMs as the permanent gatekeepers of the drug supply chain even while cutting into their revenue.
The bill would end clawbacks and prevent PBMs from cutting pharmacy reimbursement to offset federal payment changes, addressing pharmacies that often fill prescriptions below cost.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employers that buy drug coverage
industries.note: Plans would receive 100% of rebates and price concessions and full disclosure of PBM fees, so they could see and negotiate what they are actually paying.

The bill would require disclosure of all payments PBMs receive from manufacturers and direct a government study of whether formularies favor high-rebate drugs over cheaper alternatives, pressuring the rebate system; but it would not ban rebates, which many manufacturers rely on to protect list prices.
